title: The five, the four, the forty
hook: it remembers the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty liberated

segments.voice: Yesterday: jot, and your line: the ten in one, the light of ten Gurus in the Granth. Now the Ardas turns from the Gurus to the Sikhs who stood with them.

Three numbers. Say them fast and they sound like a phone number: five, four, forty. Each one is a group of people. One group stepped forward when everyone else stepped back. One was four brothers, two of them still small boys. One walked away from their Guru, and then came back. The Ardas says all three numbers in a single breath, right after the Guru Granth Sahib, before any other Sikhs it remembers.
screen: `FIVE, FOUR, FORTY.` → `THREE GROUPS OF PEOPLE.` → `SAID IN ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The line goes: panjaan piaariaan, chauhaan sahibzaadiaan, chaaleeaan mukteaan. The five beloved, the four princes, the forty liberated. The five are the Panj Pyare. At Vaisakhi at Anandpur, Sikh tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh stood before a huge gathering with a sword and asked for someone willing to give their head. A long silence. Then one man stood. Then four more. As the story is told, they came from different castes and regions: a shopkeeper, a farmer, a water carrier, a washerman, a barber. They were the first initiated into the Khalsa, and Sikhs say the Guru then asked them to initiate him. Ever since, five initiated Sikhs lead the amrit ceremony. The four are the Sahibzade, the Guru's sons. The older two, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, died fighting at Chamkaur. The younger two, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, still small boys, were captured and executed at Sirhind after, tradition says, refusing to give up their faith. Sikhs mark their martyrdom every year. The forty are the Chali Mukte. During the siege of Anandpur, a group of Sikhs left the Guru and, tradition says, signed a paper disowning him. At home they were shamed for it, and a woman named Mai Bhago led them back. They fought at Khidrana, now Muktsar, and fell. As the last of them lay dying, the story goes, the Guru tore up the paper. That's why they're called mukte, the liberated. Five who stepped forward, four who held on, forty who came back: Sikhs hear in them three ways a person can be faithful.
screen: `THE FIVE: WHO STOOD UP.` · `THE FOUR: THE GURU'S SONS.` · `THE FORTY: WHO CAME BACK.` · `THREE WAYS TO BE FAITHFUL.` · then, large: `FIVE, FOUR, FORTY.`

segments.voice: On one out-breath, say five, and picture people standing up in a silent crowd; on the next, four, and picture four brothers, two grown and two small; on the next, forty, people walking back toward someone they'd left. Repeat it slowly, and notice which you understand best right now: stepping forward, holding on, or coming back. If you pray, follow with Waheguru.
The five. The Panj Pyare who stood up, the four Sahibzade, and the forty who came back: remembered in one breath.
Your line: five, four, forty. Three numbers, three groups, said in one breath. That's day six hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty Muktas in one line; five initiated Sikhs still lead every amrit ceremony, and the Sahibzade's martyrdom is marked each year.

chat.says: At the gurdwara the prayer said 'five, four, forty.' Who are they?
options: The five who first stood up for the Khalsa, the Guru's four sons, and forty who left, then came back.
The first five Gurus, four holy cities, and forty saints whose hymns fill the scripture.
Five who fell at Chamkaur, four who signed the paper, and forty who were the first Khalsa.
chat.meaning: The Ardas remembers the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the Chali Mukte, the forty who came back: three ways to be faithful.

Panj Pyare.meaning: the five beloved, first initiated into the Khalsa

Sahibzade.meaning: the four sons of Guru Gobind Singh

Chali Mukte.meaning: the forty liberated, who left and came back

Mai Bhago.meaning: the woman who led the forty back

Vaisakhi.meaning: the spring festival when the Khalsa was founded

sources.ref: Ardas, as set out in the Sikh Rehat Maryada (SGPC)

notes: Occupations of the Panj Pyare (shopkeeper, farmer, water carrier, washerman, barber) as commonly told: confirm.
Sahibzade dates and ages (Chamkaur December 1704; Zorawar Singh about nine, Fateh Singh about six, at Sirhind): some sources give 1705; confirm.
Story of the bedava (disclaimer) torn up for Mahan Singh at Khidrana: traditional; confirm.
Oldest Sahibzada 'about eighteen' (Ajit Singh, born 1687): confirm.
